h1: Aerating wort at home by shaking, splashing or pure oxygen
title: Aerating Wort at Home | Craft Beer School
desc: Shaking, splashing or pure oxygen: how much oxygen homebrew yeast needs at pitching, what each method achieves and when dry yeast needs none.
teaser: Yeast needs oxygen at the start and none after. Here is how much each home method delivers and when it is enough.
standfirst: Oxygen is good for wort at pitching and bad for beer at every stage after. Getting enough in at the start gives yeast a healthy fermentation. Here is how shaking, splashing and pure oxygen compare.
sections: Why yeast needs oxygen at the start

When yeast is pitched, it does not start fermenting straight away. First it grows. To build new cell walls it needs sterols and unsaturated fatty acids. Making those takes oxygen. Without enough, the yeast grows less, ferments more slowly and is more likely to stall or leave off-flavours.

The oxygen is used up in the first hours. After that the yeast ferments anaerobically. From then on oxygen is only a problem. That is why aeration happens once at pitching and never again. Our guide on pitching yeast properly covers the other half of a healthy start.

Brewing texts commonly put the target for ales at around 8 to 10 parts per million of dissolved oxygen. Lagers and high gravity worts want more, often 10 to 12 ppm, because they need more yeast growth.

Air contains about 21% oxygen. Wort saturated with air at fermentation temperature holds roughly 8 ppm. That ceiling is the key fact. No amount of shaking with air can push past saturation. Pure oxygen can, because it is five times more concentrated than the oxygen in air.

Shaking is free and effective. Seal the fermenter with a sanitised lid or bung, hold it firmly and rock it hard. Air in the headspace mixes into the wort.

A couple of minutes of vigorous shaking brings cool wort close to air saturation. It works well for standard ales up to about 1.060. The practical limit is your arms and the fermenter. A full 20 litre glass carboy is heavy and slippery, so shaking glass is risky. Plastic buckets and PET carboys are safer. Leave enough headspace for air to mix.

Shake before pitching, not after. Yeast added to wort and then shaken hard works fine, but shaking first means you can check the temperature one last time with the lid off and pitch into wort that is already full of air. Keep the lid sanitised and close it before you start.

Splashing aerates during the transfer from kettle to fermenter. Let the wort fall from a height into the fermenter, or run it through a spray attachment on the end of the tube. The falling stream breaks into droplets and picks up air.

Splashing adds some oxygen but rarely reaches saturation on its own. Many homebrewers combine it with a short shake once the fermenter is full. A sanitised whisk or paddle on an electric drill also works, as long as everything touching the wort is properly sanitised first.

Pure oxygen from a small regulator and a cylinder is the most effective method. Gas runs through a sanitised stainless diffusion stone at the bottom of the fermenter. The stone's tiny pores make fine bubbles that dissolve quickly.

Run it at a low flow, enough for a gentle stream of fine bubbles, for about 60 seconds in a 20 litre batch as a starting point. Too much oxygen is possible and can increase ester production or stress the yeast. Oxygen cylinders need care. Keep them away from oil, grease and flames. Store them upright and secured. Our guide to homebrew safety with cylinders covers handling.

Dry yeast is produced in a way that loads the cells with sterol reserves. Yeast makers generally state that a fresh, rehydrated dry yeast pitch does not need wort aeration for the first fermentation. Many brewers aerate anyway as insurance. It does no harm at pitching.

For liquid yeast, a starter or a repitched slurry, aeration matters more. So does it for strong beers above about 1.070, where the yeast faces more stress. Matching oxygen to yeast type and gravity is one of the fermentation decisions we work through on our fundamentals course.

Once the yeast has started fermenting, oxygen stales the beer. It produces cardboard and sherry flavours and fades hop aroma. Do not shake, splash or open fermenters unnecessarily from about 12 hours after pitching. Transfers to bottles or kegs should be as gentle as possible. Our guide to closed transfers explains how to keep oxygen out.

For your next batch, cool the wort to pitching temperature, seal the fermenter and shake it hard for two full minutes before pitching. Note the lag time before activity. Compare it with your last batch.
faqs: How long should I shake my fermenter to aerate wort?
A couple of minutes of vigorous shaking brings cool wort close to air saturation, about 8 ppm.
Do I need to aerate wort for dry yeast?
Yeast makers generally say rehydrated dry yeast carries enough sterols for its first fermentation. Many brewers aerate anyway as insurance.
Can I add too much oxygen?
Yes, with pure oxygen. Run it gently for about a minute in a 20 litre batch as a starting point.
